links.note: 871 says enmity, a thing without good in it (பண்பிலதனை), is not to be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று). 867 says the enmity of one who stays close and does unfitting things must certainly be got, even by paying for it (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற). The conflict holds if 871 is read as a rule about all enmity; Parimelazhagar narrows it to enmity that brings no benefit, which would leave room for 867.

871 denies that enmity should be wanted at all (வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று), even playfully. 861 tells the ruler to avoid opposing the strong but to favour enmity toward the weak without holding back (ஓம்பா மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). On a plain reading one verse forbids desiring what the other recommends desiring; the two sit in adjacent chapters on enmity.

871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும்) and calls it பண்பிலது, a thing without good quality. 995 says scorn hurts even in jest (நகையுள்ளும் இன்னாது இகழ்ச்சி) and that those who know how others feel keep பண்பு even within enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள). The same three words, jest, enmity and பண்பு, are arranged differently: 871 sets enmity outside good character, 995 allows character to persist inside it.

872 says that even if you take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow (வில்லேர் உழவர்), you should not take on that of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). 129 says a wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not. Both rank harm done by words above harm done by a physical instrument, one in statecraft and one in personal conduct.

872 warns against making enemies of those who work with the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be ministers skilled in the treatises. 647 says that one who can speak, does not slip and does not fear is hard for anyone to defeat in a contest (இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 647 supplies a reason for 872's warning: such an opponent cannot easily be beaten.

873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more witless than the deranged. 450 uses the same phrase as its yardstick: giving up the tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). Read together, 450 takes the folly that 873 puts beyond madness and names something it ranks worse.

873 states the folly of standing alone (தமியனாய்) against many enemies. 875 gives the working rule for the smallest such case: with no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்), make one of them a pleasing ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க). 875 turns 873's condemnation into a remedy.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பண்புடையாளன் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on those of character (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்), and would otherwise sink into the earth. Both make பண்பு the thing the world stands on; 874, in the chapter on enmity, specifies it as the capacity to turn enemies into friends.

874 praises the one who takes enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்) without saying how it is done. 985 names a means: bowing (பணிதல்) is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Parimelazhagar glosses this as ending the opponents' enmity, so 985 reads as the method behind 874.

874 commends treating enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 830 says that when the time comes for an enemy to be a friend (பகைநட்பாம் காலம்), one should befriend with the face, keep the heart apart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ), and then drop it. The two begin with nearly the same words, and 830 limits how far the friendship of 874 should be allowed to reach inward when it is the enemy who is doing the befriending.

875 says that one with no ally and two enemies should take one of the two as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). 679 says that winning over those not attached to one's side (ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்) is more urgent than doing good to friends; Parimelazhagar takes these to be those not attached to one's enemy. Both treat recruiting from outside one's own camp as the first move when facing an enemy.

875 advises a ruler caught alone between two enemies to make one of them an ally. 633 lists among a minister's abilities dividing (பிரித்தல்), which Parimelazhagar explains as separating the enemy's supporters from him, and rejoining those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). The advice to the king in 875 is the skill required of the minister in 633.

876 says that whether or not one has trusted the enemy before, in a time of ruin (அழிவின்கண்) one should neither join him nor break from him (தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்); Parimelazhagar explains that joining lets him destroy from inside and breaking makes him add to the ruin. 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது). Both prescribe a deliberate middle distance from a dangerous party, once toward an enemy and once toward one's own king.

877 says not to let softness show before enemies (மேவற்க மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து); Parimelazhagar takes மென்மை as lack of strength, which enemies watch for. 440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without that love being known (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' designs come to nothing (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்). In both, what an enemy can use is what he is allowed to learn about one's inner state, weakness in one verse and desire in the other.

877 begins by saying not to voice one's pain to those who do not know it (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு); Parimelazhagar takes these to be friends who have not perceived it themselves. In 1200 the woman tells her heart that it means to tell its great pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and might as well try to fill the sea. The policy maxim and the lover's speech both hold that pain told to someone unconnected with it gains nothing; the love verse is a speaker's rebuke to herself, not a rule.

878 says that knowing the way, building oneself up and guarding oneself (தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப) will end the elation on the enemies' side (பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு மாயும்); Parimelazhagar explains தற்செய்து as increasing one's wealth and forces. 759 says to make wealth, since no steel is sharper for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு). Both aim at the enemy's செருக்கு, and 759 names the main material by which 878's self-strengthening is done.

878 makes knowing the way and guarding oneself (வகையறிந்து ... தற்காப்ப) enough to end the enemy's pride. 493 says even those without strength become strong and win if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves (இடனறிந்து போற்றார்கண் போற்றிச் செயின்). Both pair knowledge of the conditions with self-protection, and both leave out any need for superior force.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க), because once hardened it destroys the hand of the one removing it. 674 says the remainder of a task or of an enmity (வினைபகை என்றிரண்டின் எச்சம்) scorches like the remainder of a fire; Parimelazhagar adds that it grows again afterwards. The two verses give the same reason for finishing an enemy early, one through a tree that hardens and one through embers that flare.

879 advises destroying an enemy while he is still tender, before he can hurt the one who removes him. 488 says that on meeting foes one should bear them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க) until their end-time is seen (இறுவரை காணின்), when the head goes down. 488 covers the case 879 leaves out: an enemy who is already hardened is to be waited out, not cut.

879 speaks of those who remove the thorn tree with the word களையுநர், weeders. 550 compares a king's putting the cruel to death to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). Both picture the removal of dangerous people as a cultivator's weeding; 879 adds that timing matters, since the weed grown hard injures the weeder's hand.

880 says those who do not break the pride of those hostile to them are not alive even to breathe (உயிர்ப்ப உளரல்லர்); Parimelazhagar offers a second reading, that they die the moment their enemies so much as breathe. 763 says a sea of hostile rats perishes when the cobra merely breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). On that second reading the two verses use the same figure, an opponent destroyed by a breath, and 880 warns that a negligent ruler ends up in the rats' position.

880 states the cost of not breaking the pride of one's enemies (செயிர்ப்பவர் செம்மல் சிதைக்கலாதார்): one cannot be counted as living. 759 names the instrument for that task: wealth, the sharpest steel for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு). One verse gives the necessity and the other the means.

881 says even shade and water are bad when they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so is the nature of one's own people when it does harm. In 1309 the man says water is sweet in the shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. Both take shade and water as the standard of what is pleasant and then make the pleasantness depend on a condition, which in both cases is the real disposition of those closest to one.

881 says the nature of one's own people is bad if it does harm (தமர்நீரும் இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்). 522 says kin whose affection does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம்) yield many gains that keep branching; Parimelazhagar notes that this wording is chosen to exclude inner enmity. The condition written into 522 is the case 881 describes, so each verse marks the limit of the other.

882 says not to fear enemies who are like a sword, but to fear the bond with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி); Parimelazhagar explains that open enemies can be guarded against. Both rank the declared enemy as the lesser danger and the trusted insider as the greater.

882 contrasts the enemy who is like a drawn sword (வாள்போல் பகைவர்) with the one who looks like kin, and fears the second. 828 says a weapon hides even within an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. In 882 the visible sword is the safer one; 828 shows where the other sword is kept.

882 uses the verb of fear for kin-like enemies (அஞ்சுக கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 824 uses it for deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப்படும்). The chapter on false friendship and the chapter on inner enmity reach the same instruction: what is to be feared is hostility presented as closeness.

883 says to fear inner enmity and guard oneself, for at the moment of faltering (உலைவிடத்து) it cuts surely, like the tool that cuts the potter's clay (மட்பகை). 821 says the friendship of those who associate without inner consent (நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு) is an anvil for striking once they find the right place (சீரிடம் காணின்). Both describe a concealed enemy as a workshop tool that does its damage only when the moment arrives.

883 says to fear the enemy within and guard oneself (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க), or it will destroy one. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க); unguarded, anger kills oneself. The same formula of self-guarding against something lodged inside is applied in one verse to people within the household or court and in the other to a passion within the mind.

884 says that if an inner enmity of unreformed mind appears, it gives many ills (ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்) that spoil one's circle (இனமாணா). 522 says that if kin of unfailing affection are had, they give many gains (ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்) that keep branching. The two couplets have the same frame with opposite contents, kin as the source of many gains or of many harms depending on what lies within them.

885 says an inner enmity that comes in the form of kinship (உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை) brings many ills of a deadly kind (இறல்முறையான் ஏதம்) to the ruler. 735 defines a land as one without many factions, without ruinous inner enmity (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை) and without murderous marauders who harass the king. The danger 885 describes for the king's person and household is, in 735, something whose absence is part of what makes a country a country.

886 says that if disunity arises among those who are one with a ruler (ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின்), it is always hard for him to escape perishing. 764 defines an army as one that is not destroyed, cannot be undermined from within (அறைபோகாதாகி) and has inherited hardness. Both treat the loyalty of one's own side as a condition of survival, stated once as a warning and once as a requirement.

887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined, though it joins like a casket and its lid (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship is what makes the heart within smile (நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). Both deny the name of union to a joining that is only on the surface, in the family and in friendship.

887 uses the casket and its lid for a family that fits together outwardly while divided within. 277 uses the kunri seed for false ascetics, red on the outside (புறங்குன்றி கண்டனையர்) and black within like its tip. Each verse chooses an everyday object to show an outside that does not match the inside, one for kin and one for renouncers.

888 says a family with inner enmity wears down in strength (உரம் தேயும்) like பொன் rubbed by a file (அரம்பொருத பொன்போல); Parimelazhagar takes பொன் here as iron. 567 says harsh words and excessive punishment are the file that wears away a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). The file stands in both for slow loss of strength from one's own side, caused by hidden hatred in one verse and by the king's own harshness in the other.

889 says that inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. 965 says even those like a hill will be lowered if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). Both use a tiny seed as the measure of something that brings down what is large, a family or kingdom in 889 and a person's standing in 965.

889 holds that inner enmity is ruinous even at the size of a split sesame seed. 433 says those who are ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed (தினைத்துணை) to be as large as a palmyra. 433 describes the attitude that 889 calls for: treating the small thing at its eventual size.

889 says inner enmity carries ruin even when it is as small as a split sesame seed. 879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young (இளைதாக), since grown hard it destroys the cutter's hand. The two neighbouring chapters, on open and on inner enmity, make the same point that hostility should be judged by what it will grow into; only 879 goes on to say what to do about it.

890 says living together with those not in accord with one (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) is like sharing a hut with a snake (குடங்கருள் பாம்போடு உடனுறைந்தற்று). 825 says those not settled toward one in mind (மனத்தின் அமையாதவரை) are not to be trusted in anything on the strength of their words. 825 states the rule about trust; 890 adds what closeness to such people amounts to, with Parimelazhagar noting that the small space and constant contact make harm certain.
